clue.text: Serious lack of comic scripts

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a grave business, not to be laughed at
second meaning, read literally: no material for jokes

explanation.surface: A comedy show in trouble because its writers have delivered nothing funny.
explanation.walkthrough: Matter here is material, as in reading matter, so the phrase literally means there is nothing to joke with.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something grave that must be treated soberly, an exact match for the adjective.

clue.text: The bar, of course

parts.note: surface reading: naturally, it is the pub; setter's reading: the bar belonging to a golf course, visited after the eighteen holes are played

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like the filler 'naturally'; it means the golf course, whose clubhouse bar golfers count as one more hole after the eighteenth.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers call the clubhouse bar this, since they head there once the eighteenth green is finished.

clue.text: Desert springs keep them going

parts.note: surface reading: oases with water sustain travellers in the desert; setter's reading: springs are leaps, and these desert rodents get about by hopping on long hind legs

explanation.walkthrough: Springs look like water sources in an oasis; they are the bounding jumps of small desert animals.
explanation.definitionFit: These small long-legged rodents of African and Asian deserts move by kangaroo-like hops.

clue.text: Board and lodging's cheaper with controls

parts.note: keep is the cost of board and lodging; with the 's it reads 'keep is'
prices that are down are cheaper

explanation.surface: A landlady advertising lower rent for rooms, with house rules attached.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain or suppress something, such as costs or a rebellion, is to hold it in check.

clue.text: In use, can turn into a problem

indicators.note: to turn into something else is to change form, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: the letters as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tin that is useful can become troublesome once it is being used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word but belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A pest or annoyance is a bother, a troublesome thing or person causing difficulty.

clue.text: Handy reference book

definitions.meaning: first meaning: done or worked by hand
second meaning: a book of instructions

explanation.walkthrough: Handy reads as 'convenient', describing the book; it is a separate meaning, 'by hand'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for work done with the hands and a noun for an instruction handbook.

clue.text: Drunk in snug

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy in the snug, the small private room of a British pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A snug is a cosy side room in a British pub, which makes the drinker picture convincing; here it simply means close-fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal for intoxicated and also describes clothing that fits closely without slack.

clue.text: Receiver heading for one's home — it''s serious!

parts.note: the ear receives sound
a nest is a bird's home, and by extension anyone's

explanation.surface: Someone with a telephone receiver heading home, insisting the matter is grave.
explanation.walkthrough: Receiver suggests a telephone handset; it is the organ of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest means sincere and intensely grave in intention, a synonym for the adjective in the clue.

clue.text: Soldiers on the march?

parts.note: surface reading: troops marching along; setter's reading: a march is a frontier region, so these troops are from the frontier

explanation.walkthrough: March looks like a verb of soldiering; it is the old word for borderland, as in the Welsh Marches. The unit was a British infantry regiment from the Cumbrian border.
explanation.definitionFit: This former British infantry regiment recruited in Cumberland and Westmorland, the borderland with Scotland.

clue.text: A Scandinavian wearing no make-up

indicators.note: make-up as a noun means composition, so the preceding letters are made up afresh in another order

parts.note: the letters as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A natural-looking Nordic person who goes without cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: Make-up looks like cosmetics; it signals how the letters are composed.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Norway is a Scandinavian, so the nationality is an example of the broader group.

clue.text: Film actress in the dress circle

parts.note: garb is clothing
the letter O is round like a circle

explanation.surface: A movie star seated in the dress circle of a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The dress circle is a theatre's first balcony, so the phrase reads as one place; split it into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Greta Garbo was the Swedish-born Hollywood star of Ninotchka and Grand Hotel.

clue.text: They may be used to make a stool

definitions.text: They may be used to make a stool

parts.words: They may be used to make a stool
parts.note: read plainly: saws and hammers for building a seat; the setter's reading: the implements' own name, its letters reordered, makes the seat named next

explanation.walkthrough: Read plainly it is a carpenter's kit; the twist is that the answer's five letters can be rearranged into STOOL.
explanation.definitionFit: Implements such as saws, chisels and hammers are what a carpenter uses to build furniture.

clue.text: Old colour scheme

parts.note: surface reading: a dated decorating palette; setter's reading: a former political system dividing people by skin colour

explanation.walkthrough: Colour scheme suggests interior decoration; it is South Africa's former system of racial segregation, ended in the early 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: South Africa's segregation policy separated people by race, so it was literally a scheme based on colour.

clue.text: Establish oneself in women's concerns

indicators.note: in says the wanted letters sit inside the following words, running across their join

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Settling oneself in the area of women's issues, as a campaigner might.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle oneself firmly and comfortably in a place or position is the reflexive sense of this verb.

clue.text: His leader expresses his opinion

parts.note: surface reading: a boss speaks for a subordinate; setter's reading: a leader is a newspaper's leading article, voicing the view of the person who runs the paper

explanation.walkthrough: Leader looks like a boss; in British newspapers it is the leading article, in which the paper's chief states his view.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper writes or directs its leading articles, which voice the paper's opinion.

clue.text: Run away twice? Not this soldier!

parts.note: to desert is to abandon one's post
the same phrase taken a second time: to rat is to run out on one's side

explanation.surface: A soldier who would never flee, even when urged to do so twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The Desert Rats were the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa in the Second World War; the joke is that both halves of their name mean flee.
explanation.definitionFit: A Desert Rat was a member of the 7th Armoured Division, famed for fighting in the North African desert.

clue.text: He does his writing in bars

definitions.text: He does his writing in bars

parts.words: He does his writing in bars
parts.note: surface reading: a writer who works in pubs; setter's reading: bars are the measures into which written music is divided

explanation.walkthrough: Bars suggests pubs, or prison; it means the measures of a musical score.
explanation.definitionFit: One who writes music sets it down on staves divided into measures, so his work is literally in bars.

clue.text: He should honour his agreement to the letter

definitions.text: He should honour his agreement to the letter

parts.words: He should honour his agreement to the letter
parts.note: surface reading: someone must keep a contract precisely; setter's reading: the letter is the one who lets a property, the landlord, to whom the agreement is owed

explanation.walkthrough: 'To the letter' looks like 'exactly'; the letter is a landlord, one who lets.
explanation.definitionFit: A renter occupies property under a lease and owes its terms to the landlord who lets it.

clue.text: Warn off Harry — it may have a tusk!

indicators.note: off as in gone off or out of order, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Hal is a familiar form of Harry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

explanation.surface: A warning to a man called Harry to keep clear, as something dangerous with a tusk is about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warn off' reads as a phrasal verb; off is the signal to rearrange the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The male of this Arctic whale grows a single long spiral tusk, so the description fits it.

clue.text: Fool's speech in production of Lear

definitions.meaning: second meaning: what Edward Lear wrote, his famous verse

explanation.surface: The Fool's lines in a staging of King Lear, Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the Fool in King Lear; the Lear meant is Edward Lear, author of The Owl and the Pussy-cat and nonsense verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish talk is meaningless babble, and Edward Lear's verses are the classic example of the comic literary genre.

clue.text: Getting approval from the head?

parts.note: surface reading: a pupil winning the headteacher's favour; setter's reading: the head is the body part, which bobs to signal yes

explanation.walkthrough: The head looks like a headteacher; it is the literal head, giving approval by dipping up and down.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipping the head briefly is the usual gesture of agreement, so the participle describes giving assent.

clue.text: He is taken in by a bearded Indian chief of the desert

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being enclosed within it

parts.note: Sikh men traditionally leave their beards uncut
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man fooled by a bearded Indian man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being deceived; here it means enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: An Arab sheikh is the head of a tribe or family, so he is a chief of desert peoples.

clue.text: Taken in hand by the stockholder?

definitions.text: Taken in hand by the stockholder?

parts.words: Taken in hand by the stockholder?
parts.note: surface reading: shares managed by an investor; setter's reading: a holder of livestock, a rider or stockman, who carries a whip for his mount

explanation.walkthrough: Stockholder suggests a shareholder; read it as one who holds stock, that is animals, and the thing in his hand is a riding whip.
explanation.definitionFit: A whip for driving horses is carried in the hand by riders and drovers who tend livestock.

clue.text: Not late, but nearly lost a point

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so a piece is removed from the word before it

parts.note: taken as written
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone who was almost late, only just making it on time.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points N, S, E and W are a common crossword source of single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving before the expected time is the opposite of arriving late, so the antonym phrase defines it.

clue.text: Bones placed in a circle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: forearm bones, plural of radius
second meaning: lines drawn from a circle's centre to its edge

explanation.surface: Bones laid out in a ring, as in some ritual.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is a forearm bone and also a centre-to-edge line of a circle; the word is the plural of both.

clue.text: Hard-hearted king whose widow was merry

indicators.note: hearted says the first piece is placed at the heart of the second

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic monarch
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A cruel monarch whose bereaved wife was glad to see him go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-hearted' reads as callous; split it into hard and hearted. Franz Lehár composed the operetta The Merry Widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Lehár wrote The Merry Widow, so the widow belonging to him is the merry one in his operetta's title.

clue.text: Double description of a batman?

parts.note: surface reading: a superhero with two identities; setter's reading: a batman is an army officer's personal servant, so he is both a domestic servant and serving in the forces

explanation.walkthrough: Batman suggests the caped crusader; in the British army a batman is an officer's orderly, and the phrase describes him twice: employed as a servant, and serving in the army.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both working as a domestic servant and on active military duty, and a batman is both.

clue.text: Takes part in games of hide-and-seek?

definitions.text: Takes part in games of hide-and-seek?

parts.words: Takes part in games of hide-and-seek?
parts.note: surface reading: joining in a children's game; setter's reading: the coy game of a suitor being led on and kept at a distance

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the playground game; the meaning is the courtship game of seeming uninterested to keep a pursuer keen.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes feigning disinterest in an admirer, a flirtatious game of evasion and pursuit.
